newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israeli shares end higher led by small firms.
newsitem.headline: Israeli shares end higher led by small firms.

text.p: Israeli shares closed higher on Monday led by a sharp rise in small-capitalisation shares, traders said.
The benchmark Mishtanim index of the top 100 shares gained 0.92 percent, or 2.82 points, to 309.70 on all-share turnover of 216 million shekels against 205 million shekels on Sunday.
The Maof 25 blue chip index closed 0.95 percent higher at 317.35.

"The market is very optimistic and volume is high. Today's rise was led by the small capitalisation shares (traded on the Karam index)," said Ran Ben-Naftaly, senior investment manager at Jerusalem Capital Markets.
"Among the Karam shares, companies that are expected to offer convertible bonds in the next few weeks were the main gainers," Ben-Naftaly said.
He said that foreign investors were also showing optimism and the continued rise of Wall Street is adding to the market strength. "The only negative impact is the fear from another attack," he said.

Israel suspended dormant peace talks with the Palestinans after double suicide bombings by Moslem militants last week killed 13 people in the heart of Jewish west Jerusalem. Israel also barred tens of thousands of Palestinians from reaching their jobs in the Jewish state.

"The market continues to rise and the mood is very optimistic," said a trader at the First International Bank of Israel. "The recovery of the primary market, the decline of yields on long-CPI-linked bonds and the high activity of foreign investors all add to investors positive mood," he said.
He added that the small-capitalisation shares were becoming more attractive. "Much money comes into Karam mutual funds and this leads to sharp gains," he said.

Teva Pharmaceutical Industries, the most active share, lost 1.5 percent to 20,807 agorot (Israeli cents) on volume of 20.5 million shekels after a report on a local financial news wire said the government was demanding Teva pay an "enormous amount" in back payments of value added tax (VAT).
Teva's chief financial officer Dan Suesskind said the amount demanded was $4 million. He said the sum was "not a huge amount" for Teva and added that the government claim was without merit.
Earlier on Monday the company said earnings in the second quarter jumped to $0.55 a share, in line with analysts' expectations, against $0.01 a share a year earlier.
The 1996 quarter included a one-time expense of $0.24 a share for the acquisition of Biocraft Laboratories in May of last year.
Teva also said its treatment for multiple sclerosis is capturing the majority of new prescriptions in the United States.
IDB Holding Corp rose 3.0 percent to 8,457 agorot. Traders said the share rose on rumours that the company sold a ten percent stake to an American Investor. IDB officials would not comment.

Other active shares include Koor Industries, which closed unchanged at 39,829 agorot on turnover of 9.9 million shekels and Israel Chemicals, which rose 3.0 percent to 419 agorot on volume of 9.0 million shekels.
- Dan Gerstenfeld, Tel Aviv newsroom, 972-3-537-2211 x233
